column8: Welcome to Battles of History. Today we are learning about the Battle of Voo-ko-var, fought in the autumn of 1991 in a town on the river Danube, in eastern Croatia. On one side were the Yugoslav People's Army, the JNA, with Territorial Defence units and volunteer groups. On the other were Croatian defenders: the National Guard, the police and local volunteers. The siege lasted about three months, and when it ended the town lay in ruins. This is a recent war, and people in Croatia and in Serbia still feel it deeply. We will tell you what is known, and who says what.

Battle of Voo-ko-var. From late August to the eighteenth of November 1991, the JNA and the forces fighting with it besieged the town of Voo-ko-var. Its defenders held out for about three months before the town fell. Thousands of people were killed or went missing, soldiers and civilians, and most of the town was destroyed. After the fall, prisoners were taken from the town's hospital and killed. An international court later judged that crime.

Yugoslavia breaks apart. Yugoslavia was a country of six republics in south-eastern Europe. Its army, the JNA, belonged to the whole federation. In 1990 and 1991 the federation came apart. On the twenty-fifth of June 1991, the parliaments of Croatia and Slovenia declared independence. The implementation of Croatia's declaration was suspended for three months. On the eighth of October, Croatia's parliament cut the remaining legal ties with Yugoslavia. About one person in eight in Croatia was a Serb. Many of them feared what an independent Croatia would mean for them. In areas with many Serbs, local leaders set up their own authorities and barricades, and armed groups formed on both sides. The JNA said it was keeping the peace and defending Yugoslavia. Croatia's government saw it as an army taking Serbia's side. At Voo-ko-var, the JNA was an attacking force.

A town on the Danube. Voo-ko-var lies where a small river, the Voo-ka, meets the Danube. Across the Danube is Serbia. In 1991 the town had about twenty-one thousand Croats and fourteen thousand Serbs, and people of other backgrounds: Hungarians, Roo-sins and others. Neighbours, classmates and families crossed these lines. It had a baroque old town, a hospital, a busy river port, and, just to the north, Bor-oh-vo Nah-sel-yeh, a factory town built around a major Yugoslav shoe factory. On a hill by the Danube road stood a tall water tower. The two sides name the battle differently. In Croatia it is the defence of Voo-ko-var. In 1991, the JNA and Serb leaders called its capture a liberation. This page uses neutral words: the battle, the siege, the fall.

The two sides. The attackers were the JNA, the federal army, with tanks, artillery and aircraft. With it fought the local Serb Territorial Defence and volunteer groups, among them Zhel-ko Razh-na-to-vich's Serb Volunteer Guard, known as Ar-kahn's Tigers, and a detachment linked to the Serbian politician Voy-ee-slav Sheh-shel. The CIA later estimated that more than thirty-six thousand JNA, Territorial Defence and volunteer troops were around Voo-ko-var after reinforcements. That is the CIA's estimate of the reinforced forces around Voo-ko-var, not the number fighting in one street or at one moment. The defenders were the Croatian National Guard and the police, with local volunteers and a smaller force, the Croatian Defence Forces, known as HOS. The 204th Voo-ko-var Brigade became the main military formation in the town's defence. The CIA estimated two thousand to two thousand three hundred defenders. Croatia's veterans ministry gives the brigade a strength of about eighteen hundred. These numbers count different things at different times. They are not a head-to-head count of the two sides.

How this page tells it. This war is recent. Croatian and Serbian accounts often disagree, and some questions are still in the courts. After each line you will see a tag. "Established" means supported by reliable evidence. "ICTY finding" means the judges of the international court found it to be true. "Croatian account" or "Serbian account" tells you whose account it is. "Disputed" means the sources disagree, and "estimate" marks an approximate number. The front lines on the map are traced from a map made by the CIA in 2002, from its own research. The map of the land and the town is a painting made for this page, reconstructing the landscape and the town before the destruction. The page tells what happened to people on both sides, without graphic detail.

On the second of May, Croatian police went into Bor-oh-vo Sell-oh, a village just north of Voo-ko-var, where armed local Serbs had set up barricades. In the fighting, twelve Croatian policemen were killed. Bor-oh-vo Sell-oh, the village, is not Bor-oh-vo Nah-sel-yeh, the factory town. Through the summer, barricades went up across eastern Sla-vo-nia. The JNA and local Territorial Defence units took positions around Voo-ko-var, and inside the town, defenders organised under a series of commanders. By August, shells had already damaged the hospital's operating rooms. The Serb National Council, the council of the Serb community in Croatia, also documents killings and disappearances of Serb civilians by Croatian armed groups in Voo-ko-var before the main siege.

The twenty-fifth of August is the date usually given for the start of the battle: a large attack from several sides, and shelling almost every day from then on. At the start of September, Mee-leh Deh-dah-ko-vich, a former JNA lieutenant colonel known as Yas-treb, the Hawk, took command of the town's defence. The hospital moved its patients into the basement. Its own history notes: "Power and water sometimes fail; generators are switched on." People lived in cellars. A Croatian woman, Man-da Pat-ko, remembered: "There were days when you couldn't even come out from the basement." A Serb woman of Voo-ko-var, quoted as Kafa, remembered her street's cellar before she left on the seventh of September: "All our neighbors were in one cellar and all stuck together. Croats, Serbs and Ruthenians." A track through the corn fields still linked the town with the outside.

Across Croatia, Croatian forces began to blockade the JNA's barracks. At Voo-ko-var, the JNA attacked from the south, from the direction of Neg-oh-slav-tsee, and broke through to its own barracks in the south of the town. The barracks stayed a JNA stronghold inside the town. A JNA brigade, the 1st Guards Mechanised Brigade, held the southern edge of the town until early October. The map shows the CIA's front line for this day.

In the north, JNA armoured forces attacked from the direction of Ter-pin-ya toward Bor-oh-vo Nah-sel-yeh, down the long main road, Ter-pin-ska tses-ta. The JNA used M-84 tanks at Voo-ko-var, a Yugoslav development of the Soviet T-72. The defenders of Bor-oh-vo Nah-sel-yeh, led by Blah-go Zah-dro, fought them with mines and small teams with hand-held anti-tank weapons. Croatian veterans describe renewed attacks by "two large columns of tanks" on the eighteenth of September. In Croatia the road became known as a tank graveyard.

Around the twentieth of September, the JNA's 1st Guards Mechanised Division advanced from Sheed, in Serbia, into eastern Croatia. On the twenty-fifth, the main JNA garrison withdrew from Veen-kov-tsee, the next town to the west. In Voo-ko-var, the defenders were organised as the 204th Voo-ko-var Brigade. Not every soldier wanted this war. A Serbian human-rights group records that about two thousand reservists from Krag-oo-yeh-vats went home from Sheed. On the twenty-third of September, a reservist, Vladimir Zhiv-ko-vich, drove an armoured vehicle to the Federal Parliament in Belgrade in protest.

At the turn of September and October, the JNA reorganised its forces into two operational groups, one in the south and one in the north. Operational Group South, under Colonel Mee-leh Merk-shich, had its headquarters in a house in Neg-oh-slav-tsee. The court found that, from the eighth of October, Merk-shich alone commanded the joint combat operations of the forces in Operational Group South's area. Operational Group North was led by General Mladen Brah-tich. The core of Operational Group South was the Guards Motorised Brigade, from Belgrade. With the JNA fought the local Territorial Defence and volunteer groups. The front line, which the map shows, now held Voo-ko-var and Bor-oh-vo Nah-sel-yeh together in one pocket. On the third and fifth of October, the JNA attacked Noosh-tar, the village on the road to Veen-kov-tsee, and was pushed back.

On the first of October, the JNA captured Ma-rin-tsee and cut the road west. That blocked the main supply route. The remaining tracks through the corn fields were dangerous, and Bog-dah-nov-tsee held out as a defended pocket on the way. Croatian forces outside tried again and again to break through to the town, but could not open a lasting corridor. Deh-dah-ko-vich went out to Veen-kov-tsee to lead the relief from outside. In mid-October, Branko Bor-ko-vich, a former JNA captain, took command inside the town.

On the sixteenth of October, the JNA attacked Bor-oh-vo Nah-sel-yeh and Ter-pin-ska tses-ta from several directions at once. Blah-go Zah-dro, the commander in Bor-oh-vo Nah-sel-yeh, was killed. On the seventeenth and eighteenth, there was fighting at Loo-zhats, between Bor-oh-vo Nah-sel-yeh and the town, including over a temporary floating bridge on the Voo-ka.

For one day, a neutral medical convoy got through. It was organised with May-deh-san Son Fron-tyair, Doctors Without Borders. It came in from Bog-dah-nov-tsee along a narrow road through the corn fields. MSF records that it left the hospital at twenty past eleven in the morning on the nineteenth of October, with more than a hundred wounded patients. MSF counted a hundred and nine; the hospital, a hundred and twelve. On the way out, the convoy was forced onto a different route, and a mine injured two MSF nurses. It was a single convoy, not an opened road, and the siege went on.

West of the town, the village of Bog-dah-nov-tsee guarded the corn-field route. On the twenty-ninth of October, the JNA renewed its attack on it. New Croatian units fought outside the ring, west of the town and toward Noosh-tar. The CIA later judged that the relief efforts were too weak and badly coordinated. Some people in Croatia later claimed that their own government had given Voo-ko-var up. That claim remains disputed: failed relief attempts alone do not prove an intention to abandon the town.

In early November, JNA attacks around Loo-zhats and the Danube port threatened the link between Bor-oh-vo Nah-sel-yeh and the town centre. General Mladen Brah-tich, commander of Operational Group North, was killed in early November. On the eighth and ninth, the CIA's account describes another JNA attack into Bor-oh-vo Nah-sel-yeh. A Croatian account records that on the ninth, defenders pulled back to reserve positions at Loo-zhats and Boo-jak.

On the tenth of November, Bog-dah-nov-tsee fell, and the remaining route through it was lost. The map shows the CIA's reconstruction of the front on that day, as the defence was being divided into separate pockets.

On the evening of the twelfth of November, Croatian forces outside made one last attack toward Ma-rin-tsee to break through. They had too few troops, and it failed. The CIA dates the loss of Bor-oh-vo Nah-sel-yeh's grain silo to the thirteenth. By then, the defence was breaking into separate pockets. The CIA describes the attackers' infantry, tanks and engineers working together better in this last phase. At the same time, a Serbian reporter with the attacking side, Yo-van Doo-lo-vich, described confusion among some units. He wrote in his diary on the fourteenth of November: "I don't see who's in command, who obeys who."

On the eighteenth of November, the defenders of Meet-nit-sa, in the south-east of the town, surrendered. They insisted on surrendering to the JNA, not to the Territorial Defence. The court records that the Croatian forces in the area of Voo-ko-var "capitulated on 18 November 1991". The same day, in Zagreb, an agreement provided for the hospital to be evacuated under Red Cross protection, with European monitors given access throughout. In 1991 the JNA and the Serb authorities called the day a liberation. On this page, we say the town fell. The siege had lasted about three months.

In the days after the surrender, people from the town, civilians and defenders, were gathered and questioned at Vel-eh-pro-met, a warehouse in the south of the town. Some detainees were beaten and abused there. On the nineteenth of November, the JNA's Operational Group South took control of the hospital. The European monitors were kept out, and the Red Cross was given only limited access. On the twentieth, at a bridge, Major Vess-el-in Shlyee-van-cha-nin stopped a Red Cross official, Nicolas Borsinger. The court found that he deliberately delayed the Red Cross. The hospital's director, Dr Ves-na Boss-a-nats, was questioned on the nineteenth, held overnight, and returned to the hospital the next morning. She was later imprisoned, and released in a prisoner exchange on the tenth of December. In Bor-oh-vo Nah-sel-yeh, the historian Dah-vor Mar-ee-yan dates the end of organised defence to the nineteenth of November; another account gives the twentieth for the final surrender.

The brigade's records, cited by the Croatian researchers Roo-zhich and Zhee-vich, count four hundred and twenty-two soldiers of the Voo-ko-var brigade dead, four hundred and fifty-seven missing, and seven hundred and seventy-seven wounded, in that historical record. Some books add the dead and the missing together. A Croatian study, Dimensions of the Crime in Voo-ko-var in 1991, cited by Roo-zhich and Zhee-vich, gives about eleven hundred civilians killed in Voo-ko-var. Using incomplete Serb records, Croatian researchers listed three hundred and fifty Serb residents of the former Voo-ko-var municipality: two hundred and three Territorial Defence members, including six listed as missing, and a hundred and forty-seven civilians recorded as dead, in 1991. This is not a count of everyone killed by Croatian forces. Published estimates of the JNA's losses differ widely, and this page does not choose one total. These numbers come from different counts, so they cannot be added together. Ov-chara. On the twentieth of November, buses carrying prisoners left the hospital at about ten in the morning. Most of the prisoners were men, and many were wounded defenders. They were driven to the JNA barracks, and from there, between one and two in the afternoon, to a hangar on the Ov-chara farm, outside Voo-ko-var. Prisoners were beaten at the hangar. That evening, no later than nine o'clock, the JNA guard was withdrawn on Colonel Merk-shich's order. That night, members of the local Territorial Defence and of volunteer units killed the prisoners and buried them in a mass grave. In 1996, two hundred bodies were recovered from the grave. In 2007, the court found that a hundred and ninety-four named victims in this case had been murdered there. They were prisoners, and the law protected them from being killed. After the capture, many non-Serb residents were forced to leave Voo-ko-var. Thousands of prisoners from Croatia, many of them from Voo-ko-var, were held in camps in Serbia, such as Srem-ska Mee-tro-vit-sa and Stah-yee-cheh-vo. The Humanitarian Law Center in Belgrade has documented how badly they were treated. At the international court in The Hague, Mee-leh Merk-shich was sentenced to twenty years. Mee-ro-slav Rah-dich, a company commander, was acquitted. Vess-el-in Shlyee-van-cha-nin's sentence was raised on appeal, when he was also convicted of aiding and abetting murder. In 2010, after new evidence, a review overturned that murder conviction; his final sentence was ten years, for aiding and abetting torture. Slobodan Mee-lo-sheh-vich, Serbia's president, and Goran Hah-jich, the local Serb leader, died before their trials ended, so those trials ended without verdicts on their guilt. Courts in Belgrade later convicted others for Ov-chara. For the next four years, Voo-ko-var was held by the Serb authorities in this part of Croatia. From January 1996, a United Nations mission ran the region. On the fifteenth of January 1998 the mission ended, and the region completed its peaceful return to Croatian administration. Years later, a JNA veteran, Mee-leh Mee-lo-sheh-vich, talked to a reporter about the war. He asked: "Did it have to be that way?" Each November, on the eighteenth, a large remembrance procession walks from the hospital to the Memorial Cemetery in Voo-ko-var. In Serbia there is no single view: some still call the battle a liberation, while Serbian human-rights groups and journalists remember the victims. The water tower was restored and opened as a memorial, with its shell damage kept. It stands over the Danube as a symbol of the town.

Croatian forces outside tried again and again to break through to the town, but could not open a lasting corridor. Deh-dah-ko-vich went out to Veen-kov-tsee to lead the relief from outside. In mid-October, Branko Bor-ko-vich, a former JNA captain, took command inside the town.

On the sixteenth of October, the JNA attacked Bor-oh-vo Nah-sel-yeh and Ter-pin-ska tses-ta from several directions at once. Blah-go Zah-dro, the commander in Bor-oh-vo Nah-sel-yeh, was killed. On the seventeenth and eighteenth, there was fighting at Loo-zhats, between Bor-oh-vo Nah-sel-yeh and the town, including over a temporary floating bridge on the Voo-ka.

For one day, a neutral medical convoy got through. It was organised with May-deh-san Son Fron-tyair, Doctors Without Borders. It came in from Bog-dah-nov-tsee along a narrow road through the corn fields. MSF records that it left the hospital at twenty past eleven in the morning on the nineteenth of October, with more than a hundred wounded patients. MSF counted a hundred and nine; the hospital, a hundred and twelve. On the way out, the convoy was forced onto a different route, and a mine injured two MSF nurses. It was a single convoy, not an opened road, and the siege went on.

West of the town, the village of Bog-dah-nov-tsee guarded the corn-field route. On the twenty-ninth of October, the JNA renewed its attack on it. New Croatian units fought outside the ring, west of the town and toward Noosh-tar. The CIA later judged that the relief efforts were too weak and badly coordinated. Some people in Croatia later claimed that their own government had given Voo-ko-var up. That claim remains disputed: failed relief attempts alone do not prove an intention to abandon the town.

In early November, JNA attacks around Loo-zhats and the Danube port threatened the link between Bor-oh-vo Nah-sel-yeh and the town centre. General Mladen Brah-tich, commander of Operational Group North, was killed in early November. On the eighth and ninth, the CIA's account describes another JNA attack into Bor-oh-vo Nah-sel-yeh. A Croatian account records that on the ninth, defenders pulled back to reserve positions at Loo-zhats and Boo-jak.

On the tenth of November, Bog-dah-nov-tsee fell, and the remaining route through it was lost. The map shows the CIA's reconstruction of the front on that day, as the defence was being divided into separate pockets.

On the evening of the twelfth of November, Croatian forces outside made one last attack toward Ma-rin-tsee to break through. They had too few troops, and it failed. The CIA dates the loss of Bor-oh-vo Nah-sel-yeh's grain silo to the thirteenth. By then, the defence was breaking into separate pockets. The CIA describes the attackers' infantry, tanks and engineers working together better in this last phase. At the same time, a Serbian reporter with the attacking side, Yo-van Doo-lo-vich, described confusion among some units. He wrote in his diary on the fourteenth of November: "I don't see who's in command, who obeys who."

On the eighteenth of November, the defenders of Meet-nit-sa, in the south-east of the town, surrendered. They insisted on surrendering to the JNA, not to the Territorial Defence. The court records that the Croatian forces in the area of Voo-ko-var "capitulated on 18 November 1991". The same day, in Zagreb, an agreement provided for the hospital to be evacuated under Red Cross protection, with European monitors given access throughout. In 1991 the JNA and the Serb authorities called the day a liberation. On this page, we say the town fell. The siege had lasted about three months.

In the days after the surrender, people from the town, civilians and defenders, were gathered and questioned at Vel-eh-pro-met, a warehouse in the south of the town. Some detainees were beaten and abused there. On the nineteenth of November, the JNA's Operational Group South took control of the hospital. The European monitors were kept out, and the Red Cross was given only limited access. On the twentieth, at a bridge, Major Vess-el-in Shlyee-van-cha-nin stopped a Red Cross official, Nicolas Borsinger. The court found that he deliberately delayed the Red Cross. The hospital's director, Dr Ves-na Boss-a-nats, was questioned on the nineteenth, held overnight, and returned to the hospital the next morning. She was later imprisoned, and released in a prisoner exchange on the tenth of December. In Bor-oh-vo Nah-sel-yeh, the historian Dah-vor Mar-ee-yan dates the end of organised defence to the nineteenth of November; another account gives the twentieth for the final surrender.

Voo-ko-var fell on the eighteenth of November 1991, after about three months of siege. Much of the town was destroyed. The brigade's records, cited by the Croatian researchers Roo-zhich and Zhee-vich, count four hundred and twenty-two soldiers of the Voo-ko-var brigade dead, four hundred and fifty-seven missing, and seven hundred and seventy-seven wounded, in that historical record. Some books add the dead and the missing together. A Croatian study, Dimensions of the Crime in Voo-ko-var in 1991, cited by Roo-zhich and Zhee-vich, gives about eleven hundred civilians killed in Voo-ko-var. Using incomplete Serb records, Croatian researchers listed three hundred and fifty Serb residents of the former Voo-ko-var municipality: two hundred and three Territorial Defence members, including six listed as missing, and a hundred and forty-seven civilians recorded as dead, in 1991. This is not a count of everyone killed by Croatian forces. Published estimates of the JNA's losses differ widely, and this page does not choose one total. These numbers come from different counts, so they cannot be added together. Ov-chara. On the twentieth of November, buses carrying prisoners left the hospital at about ten in the morning. Most of the prisoners were men, and many were wounded defenders. They were driven to the JNA barracks, and from there, between one and two in the afternoon, to a hangar on the Ov-chara farm, outside Voo-ko-var. Prisoners were beaten at the hangar. That evening, no later than nine o'clock, the JNA guard was withdrawn on Colonel Merk-shich's order. That night, members of the local Territorial Defence and of volunteer units killed the prisoners and buried them in a mass grave. In 1996, two hundred bodies were recovered from the grave. In 2007, the court found that a hundred and ninety-four named victims in this case had been murdered there. They were prisoners, and the law protected them from being killed. After the capture, many non-Serb residents were forced to leave Voo-ko-var. Thousands of prisoners from Croatia, many of them from Voo-ko-var, were held in camps in Serbia, such as Srem-ska Mee-tro-vit-sa and Stah-yee-cheh-vo. The Humanitarian Law Center in Belgrade has documented how badly they were treated. At the international court in The Hague, Mee-leh Merk-shich was sentenced to twenty years. Mee-ro-slav Rah-dich, a company commander, was acquitted. Vess-el-in Shlyee-van-cha-nin's sentence was raised on appeal, when he was also convicted of aiding and abetting murder. In 2010, after new evidence, a review overturned that murder conviction; his final sentence was ten years, for aiding and abetting torture. Slobodan Mee-lo-sheh-vich, Serbia's president, and Goran Hah-jich, the local Serb leader, died before their trials ended, so those trials ended without verdicts on their guilt. Courts in Belgrade later convicted others for Ov-chara. For the next four years, Voo-ko-var was held by the Serb authorities in this part of Croatia. From January 1996, a United Nations mission ran the region. On the fifteenth of January 1998 the mission ended, and the region completed its peaceful return to Croatian administration. Years later, a JNA veteran, Mee-leh Mee-lo-sheh-vich, talked to a reporter about the war. He asked: "Did it have to be that way?" Each November, on the eighteenth, a large remembrance procession walks from the hospital to the Memorial Cemetery in Voo-ko-var. In Serbia there is no single view: some still call the battle a liberation, while Serbian human-rights groups and journalists remember the victims. The water tower was restored and opened as a memorial, with its shell damage kept. It stands over the Danube as a symbol of the town.
